what_it_does: Running large AI language models on a phone or other edge device is hard because the model weights take too much memory and require too much arithmetic. One common fix is quantization — replacing the precise floating-point numbers that store model weights with smaller, rounded numbers — which shrinks the model and speeds up math. A popular variant called Block Floating Point (BFP) groups several numbers together and gives them one shared exponent (the 'scale' that sets their magnitude), but it must align everyone in the group to the largest number, which makes small and medium values lose precision and degrades the model's accuracy. BBAL introduces a new format called Bidirectional Block Floating Point (BBFP) that reduces how strongly the largest value in a group dominates the shared exponent, shrinking the rounding error for the rest. The paper pairs this number format with a complete chip design — including the array of math units that process these numbers and a compact circuit for the non-linear functions (like the activation gates inside the model) — to demonstrate accurate low-bit AI inference on an edge accelerator. Be appropriately hedged — the exact accuracy-versus-compression trade-off numbers come from the abstract only.
